Photograph: Dan Bashakov/AP Ukraine Russian attack on Kyiv kills at least 17 as Zelenskyy calls for better air defences Ukraine was unable to shoot down any of Russia’s missiles in assault that left 27 people injured Europe live – latest updates Guardian staff and agencies Wed 5 Aug 2026 03.58 EDT First published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 01.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russian strikes in and around Kyiv overnight killed at least 17 people, ⁠injured 27 and ⁠damaged warehouses, ​emergency service officials said. Air raid alerts lasted for more than an hour as Moscow’s forces continued deadly heavy attacks on the Ukrainian capital. Kyiv was unable to shoot down any of the missiles launched by Russia, whose intensifying attacks have prompted Kyiv to plead for more US-made Patriot interceptors. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said: “Ballistic interceptors are what could have saved the lives of those killed today.” The military administration said seven sites were hit in an assault that began on Wednesday after midnight. In Kyiv, authorities said one person died, 24 ⁠were injured and buildings were damaged. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said: “There may still be people ​under the rubble.” Rescuers pulled two people from the ruins of a warehouse near the city centre ‌that was destroyed in the attack. An ambulance driver was among the 24 injured and four people were in a critical condition, Klitschko added. He ‌said the attack set off fires in warehouses and storage areas. A ​large fire broke out on the city’s outskirts and debris from a fallen missile landed beside a residential building. Ukraine war briefing: Russian soldier in Crimea shoots comrades and civilians Read more The Kyiv military administration said the attack caused an ammonia leak that emergency crews were tackling. Witnesses heard explosions throughout the city. Klitschko said ⁠air defence units went to work against the assault. One journalist reported seeing dark smoke and the acrid smell of burning lingering in the air hours later. Natalia Reutska, who lives in Kyiv, told AFP: “The night was so terrifying, so hard,. “We’ve gotten used to waking up thinking, ’we were lucky today,’ and that’s very scary.” Ukraine shot down 98 of the 115 drones fired by Russia overnight, the air force said, but it was unable to shoot down any of the missiles, preliminary statistics showed. Kyiv can intercept the vast majority of drones, but relies on supplies from allies to counter missiles. On Wednesday, the Russian defence ministry said it had hit logistic hubs and supply centres in Kyiv and surrounding areas, claiming they were for military purposes. Russia’s military has an extensive history of striking purely civilian targets in Ukraine and committing anti-civilian atrocities . In Russia on Tuesday, Ukraine hit Wildberries logistics hubs, adding to ​more than a dozen ​it has damaged recently. Subscribe A 38-year-old Ukrainian citizen is to leave Poland after repeated alcohol-related driving offenses and breaking court bans. The case turns on deportation, but the source text does not say whether the removal has already taken place or whether the order has only been issued. - Advertisement - The reason for the move is straightforward: driving after drinking alcohol and ignoring bans imposed by a court. Those two elements matter because they show a pattern, not a single lapse, and that is what pushed the case from routine punishment into removal from Poland. Poland and the court bans The available text says only that the man repeatedly broke court bans. It does not list the bans one by one, so the legal basis has to be read in general terms: once a court order exists, violating it can escalate the consequences from a fine or restriction to expulsion. For a foreign national, that shift changes the stakes immediately. The issue is no longer only the traffic offense itself; it is repeated defiance of a court-imposed restriction, which is the part that leads to deportation in this case. Alcohol-related driving offenses The alcohol-related driving conduct is the second pillar of the case. The source says the citizen drove after drinking alcohol, and it presents that conduct as repeated, not isolated. - Advertisement - That matters for anyone following how Poland handles foreign nationals who break the law: the removal is tied to persistence. A single incident can trigger a penalty, but repeated offending combined with court-ban violations is what moves the case toward leaving Poland. What changes for the 38-year-old The immediate change is practical: the 38-year-old Ukrainian citizen is now facing removal from Poland. The wording in the source leaves a timing gap, though, so readers cannot tell from the available text whether he has already crossed the border or is still waiting for the order to be carried out. That uncertainty is the main friction in the story. The deportation headline points to an outcome, while the body text only says he is to leave Poland, which leaves open the status of the decision itself and the exact moment it will take effect. For readers tracking similar enforcement cases, the takeaway is simple. Poland can move from traffic enforcement to deportation when alcohol-related driving is paired with repeated violations of court bans, and this case shows that the removal decision can stand even before the departure itself is described. https://www.dw.com/en/india-s-young-work.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OJyY The use of AI is widespread among younger Indians, with a survey finding that 93% of Gen Z respondents and 95% of millennial respondents used AI in their day-to-day work Image: PUNIT PARANJPE/AFP/Getty Images Advertisement Across India , young workers are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI) to speed up routine tasks, whether researching news stories, translating copy, analyzing business data or sorting legal documents. But the technology can get things wrong , and relying on it too heavily carries risks. Journalist Farah Kazmi, 28, who works for a news portal in New Delhi, used AI while reporting on rules governing stray animals and feeding them in gated communities. She asked an AI model to find the Supreme Court's latest guidelines, earlier court rulings and recent dog-bite cases. "Since it can take quite a lot of time to search Google for specific articles about court rulings, previous judgments or recent dog-bite cases, I asked AI to find them for me," Kazmi told DW. It gave her a starting point for relevant articles and cases, which she then read and cross-checked herself. India's workers train AI that may replace them To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Kazmi also uses AI to translate English copy into Hindi for the Hindi news team, and Hindi quotes into English. But translations need careful checking, Kazmi said, pointing out that in one case, AI interpreted the name "Suraj" as "sun," changing the sentence's meaning. "Before using AI, I mostly relied on Google Translate. It was more literal and did not always understand the context. AI gives a much better and more context-based translation, although it still needs to be checked and corrected," she said. AI has not fundamentally changed journalism, which still involves talking to people and reporting from the field, Kazmi said. "Ultimately, I see AI as a tool that helps with research and saves time," she said, "but the actual verification and reporting still has to be done by the journalist." Yajatt Misra, 28, business strategy and international markets manager at Kanoria Chemicals and Industries, uses AI to analyze data, summarize large volumes of information, prepare first drafts and structure ideas. It also helps him turn financial and business information from different sources into management updates and presentations. "Things like summarizing information, preparing first drafts, analyzing data and putting together presentations take less time now," Misra told DW. Misra said the challenge was knowing when to trust the output. AI can miss business context or get details wrong, so its numbers, logic and conclusions need checking. "There is less need to spend time on repetitive tasks and more focus on analysis, problem-solving and providing useful insights to the business," Misra said. India's AI power play To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video A 'junior colleague' Rakshanda Deka, a 30-year-old lawyer, uses AI to sort large bundles of client documents chronologically or by theme and produce a first list of important dates. Some systems link information to the original documents so lawyers can check the source. AI can also help prepare standard applications and petitions using a lawyer's own format and style. "If used sensibly, and without outsourcing the substantive legal thinking, AI is basically like having a sincere fresher or junior colleague," Deka told DW. But AI can confidently produce false information — making human checking essential. "AI often gives you false information dressed up very confidently as fact," Deka said. "So it is imperative that you double-check everything." Deka is concerned that some young lawyers may use AI as a substitute for their own thinking. "A lot of the youngest lawyers are beginning to use AI as a substitute for themselves," she said. Widespread AI use The use of AI is widespread among younger Indians, with a survey by Deloitte this year finding that 93% of Gen Z respondents and 95% of millennial respondents used artificial intelligence in their day-to-day work. An Emeritus survey found that 82% of respondents aged 15 to 28 used AI tools at least weekly to learn or develop new skills. AI is much hyped, frequently feared, and possibly overrated To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Dimple Khubchandani, founder of recruitment firm Synoverge Consultants, told DW that employers increasingly want young professionals who can think critically, solve problems and check AI-generated work rather than simply handle basic research or drafting. "AI is not necessarily eliminating entire job categories, but it is creating leaner teams and raising expectations," she said. Khubchandani said a marketing agency that once might have hired four junior copywriters could now hire one to use AI for initial drafts, leaving more time to edit, refine the tone and shape strategy. "AI is raising the baseline capability expected from employees on day one," she said. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), one of India's largest IT services companies, said in its 2025-26 annual report that it had scaled up its "Human+AI" operating model and was embedding artificial intelligence across services and software development. Changing job market Shrijay Sheth, co-founder of LegalWiz.in, an online legal and compliance service, sees the shift across the economy. "AI's impact on job profiles isn't an anticipation," Sheth told DW. "It is a reality now. From basic research to strategy, operations, marketing, design and development, AI is changing how work gets done." In software development, Sheth said, developers are spending less time writing code from scratch and more time monitoring, testing and refining AI-generated output. "Business, product and problem-solving ability, coupled with skills around working with AI platforms, is valued over mere technical ability to work with any particular coding language," Sheth said. How AI is changing the working world To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video By the numbers The question of what happens to entry-level work is becoming harder to ignore. A 2025 report by NITI Aayog, the Indian government's public policy think tank , cites data from the Center of Advanced Study in India suggesting that more than 60% of formal-sector jobs could be susceptible to automation by 2030 — particularly in IT and business-process services. It also warns of slower hiring for entry-level software engineers and identifies junior quality-assurance and Level 1 support roles as vulnerable. The World Bank's October 2026 India Development Update says AI's long-term impact on the country's labor market remains uncertain. India could benefit from its technical workforce, IT sector and digital infrastructure, the report found, but stronger workforce skills and wider access to AI capabilities will be needed if the gains are to be broadly shared. "The productivity enhancement and job loss are both real," Sheth said. Deka said lawyers would increasingly be distinguished by how rigorously they check AI's work. "I think the differentiation is increasingly coming from the thoroughness of post-AI verification and confirmation," she said.
